timeline.text: The earliest claims later incorporated into the Camp Bird property were staked.
Thomas F. Walsh consolidated claims into the Camp Bird Mining Company and developed the property as a major operation.
A long aerial tram was built to move ore from the high mine to a lower stamp mill.
A fire destroyed the mill and a larger replacement followed.
A long haulage and drainage tunnel linked deep workings to the mill.
A 500-ton-per-day mill was completed during a later modernization period.
Regular mining operations ceased after decades of intermittent production and redevelopment.

moreHistory: Kelley and Caswell Silver describes a persistent fissure zone more than two miles long, averaging nearly 100 feet wide along the Dunmore claim.

Federal exploration records document renewed interest in the Dunmore and related Yankee Lad claims during the 1950s, including tungsten investigation.
Modern locality records document aerial-tram-station and cable remnants below the mine, but the exact present condition of every structure has not been independently field-verified.

The site was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2005 for its military, industrial, and social-history significance, with 1904 identified as its significant year.

moreHistory: The defensive site consisted of a small wooden guardhouse, a flag mount, and a stone emplacement described in period and preservation sources as a sniper or rapid-fire-gun position.
